unit.can_do_en: talk with the daycare and school about my children.

judge.reason: Same greeting and question; only register differs (moi/hei, oot sä/oletko sinä).

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.gloss_en: Yes. How is Anna doing at school?

judge.reason: Joo/kyllä and koulus/koulussa are register variants; same question about Anna at school.

lines.speaker: Mika
lines.text_puhe: Tosi hyvin. Se on hyvä matikas.
lines.text_kirja: Todella hyvin. Hän on hyvä matematiikassa.
lines.gloss_en: Really well. She's good at maths.

judge.reason: Tosi/todella, se/hän, matikas/matematiikassa are register differences; same meaning.

lines.speaker: Mika
lines.text_puhe: Se oppii nopeesti. Se puhuu jo kavereiden kaa suomee.
lines.text_kirja: Hän oppii nopeasti. Hän puhuu jo kavereiden kanssa suomea.
lines.gloss_en: She learns fast. She already speaks Finnish with her friends.

judge.reason: Se/hän, nopeesti/nopeasti, kaa/kanssa, suomee/suomea are spoken forms; same meaning.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.gloss_en: Wonderful! At home we speak Portuguese.

judge.reason: Puhutaan is the spoken form of puhumme; same fact about speaking Portuguese at home.

lines.speaker: Mika
lines.text_puhe: Se on hyvä. Kaks kieltä on rikkaus.
lines.text_kirja: Se on hyvä. Kaksi kieltä on rikkaus.
lines.gloss_en: That's good. Two languages are a gift.

judge.reason: Kaks/kaksi is the same number two; same statement.
Kiitti/kiitos are register variants of thanks.

forms.why_en: Moi is the everyday spoken hello. Books and formal texts write hei.

forms.form_name_en: present tense, 2nd person singular, with the question ending -ko/-kö
forms.why_en: In Ootsä, speech says oot for olet and joins sä to it. Books write oletko sinä.
Means 'you' (one person). Spoken: 'sä'.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Yes. In everyday speech people often say joo instead.

Pärjätä takes -ä doubled for he or she: pärjää. Miten pärjää? asks how someone copes.
Adds -ssa for 'in': koulu becomes koulussa. Speech shortens -ssa to -s: koulussa becomes koulus.
Books write todella. In speech people use tosi, 'really', instead.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Speech uses se for a person. Books write hän.
Means 'is': present tense, 3rd person singular, going with 'Helsinki'.
Means 'good!' or 'great!', showing you are happy.
Speech uses the short word matikka: matikas. Books write matematiikassa, with -ssa for 'in'.
Means 'and what about...?', turning the question back to the other person.
Suomi with -n, and i turns to e: suomen kurssi, a Finnish course.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Oppia doubles its last vowel for he or she: oppii.
Adds -sti to nopea (fast) to say how: nopeasti. Speech turns ea into ee: nopeesti.
Puhua doubles its last vowel for he or she: puhuu.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Kaveri takes -iden so it can go with kanssa (with): kavereiden kanssa.
Speech shortens kanssa to kaa. Books write kanssa.
The partitive adds -a after puhua, to speak: suomea. Speech turns -ea into -ee.
The partitive singular is used in exclamations: ihana becomes ihanaa!
Koti with -na means 'at home': kotona. The i of koti turns into o before the ending. You hear it every day.
Me means we. People say it the same way.
Books write me puhumme. Speech says me puhutaan, the same form as 'one speaks', for 'we speak'.
After puhua (to speak), a language takes -a: portugali becomes portugalia.
'It.' Nominative singular, referring back to the price.
Speech drops the final i: kaksi becomes kaks.
After a number like kaksi, the word takes -tä: kieli becomes kieltä, 'two languages'.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
